positions.commentary: Etsy struggles to re-engage users who bought in previous years, often relying on discounts like coupons or free shipping to bring them back.
Amazon maintains a strong position with Amazon Prime, making it top of mind for consumers and habituating them to check Amazon first.
DoorDash offers credits like a $10 credit when users order, which helps retain users but does not necessarily increase activity across different categories.
Lyft offers discounts like 20% off the next three rides to encourage users to return to the platform.
Alibaba historically had much higher margins of 50% plus in its earlier days, unlike current e-commerce players.
eBay has margins of 20%, which is higher than the theoretical profitability possible for Wish given its marketing spend.

thesis: The episode argues that Wish operates an unsustainable business model because it relies on heavy maintenance marketing to re-engage users who leave after a single purchase, resulting in low lifetime value relative to acquisition costs. While competitors like eBay and Alibaba demonstrate higher margins and stronger user habits, Wish's strategy of using discounts to retain customers indicates a fundamental disconnect between its value proposition and consumer desires.

claims.claim: The speaker argues Wish has an unsustainable business model because it relies heavily on maintenance marketing to retain users who leave after one purchase, resulting in low lifetime value relative to acquisition costs.
claims.quote: Whereas wish buyers buy once and are just done with them. Whatever they, that's, experience was that was not right for them and they're gone. But if you give them 50 off, then sure, sure, they'll find some crap that they could buy again. That's just such a difference, like maintenance marketing spend on those two.

claims.claim: Analysis shows Wish spends 30% to 47% of revenue on re-engagement marketing, which is unsustainable and prevents profitability compared to competitors like eBay or Alibaba.
claims.quote: We show that they're spending 47% of revenues on this quote-unquote re-engagement marketing. And some of that could be branding. And so maybe it's really more like 30%. Still, still, it is more than would ever allow them to even theoretically be profitable.

claims.claim: Wish's implied user lifetime value is only 2.3 years while customer acquisition costs are about two years, meaning the company is only skimming a thin layer of gross profit to support operations.
claims.quote: And we figured an implied lifetime value of the user was 2.3 years. So their implied lifetime values 2.3 years. And their CAQ is about two years. So that means there's 0.3 years of like gross profit. You're skimming off the top of these users.

claims.claim: Wish lost 2 million users between 2018 and 2019 while only growing revenues by 2%, despite spending 83% of revenue on sales and marketing.
claims.quote: If you look at 2018 users, were $64 million. And in 2019, they were $62 million. Okay? So they lost 2 million users. Their S&M as a percent of revenue was 83%. So 83% of revenues are spent on S&M. They lose 2 million users and they only grow their revenues 2%.

claims.claim: Wish's business model is flawed because its marketing spend is maintenance rather than growth, indicating a disconnect between the consumer value proposition and what consumers want.
claims.quote: And so the big thing here is that for Pintuwa-Duo-Dwar, almost all their marketing turned out to be growth marketing, right? Because they're actually growing with this marketing spend, whereas in contrast, wish all of this marketing spend is maintenance marketing.

claims.claim: Wish is failing because it relies on promotions to reacquire users who have already spent on the site, showing a disconnect between the consumer value prop and consumer wants.
claims.quote: What they're basically saying is that I'm not going to shop on the site unless you continue to give me 50 off promos. And there actually are plenty of these promos. I have one of them in the report where it says on the bottom, 50 off for new customers or if you haven't purchased in the last 30 days.

claims.claim: Wish spent $1.5 billion on marketing in 2019 while user count dropped by 2 million and revenue growth was only 2%, which is never a recipe for success.
claims.quote: When they spend a billion and a half on marketing in 2019 and their users are down 2 million and revenue growth is only 2%. If you were spending some 80% of your revenues for 2% revenue growth and are unprofitable, that is never going to be a recipe for success.

claims.claim: Wish's customers are not habituated to use the site because they only shop if given discounts, indicating a disconnect between the consumer value prop and what the consumer wants.
claims.quote: These are their preferences. The value prop is what the company is offering. And so To the extent that your normal business offering is not adequately hitting on enough consumer preferences, you do not have the right value prop.

claims.claim: Wish is trying to create instincts for users to shop out of boredom or for entertainment, which is exceedingly challenging.
claims.quote: I think of a product I need or I know Wish was trying to go for the entertainment, entertainment, gamification, shopping. I'm bored. I want to go to Wish. Trying to create those instincts is exceedingly challenging.
